name: cinderx (Meta CinderX JIT and Static Python for CPython)
baseline: CPython 3.x stock interpreter (version not stated in the benchmark table)
workload: Three single-process Python benchmarks (Fannkuch, Richards, nbody) timed with the JIT off versus CinderX JIT, Static Python plus JIT, and Static Python plus primitive types.
claimed_speedup: Project docs table (seconds, lower is better): Richards 3.73s No JIT vs 2.12s CinderX JIT; nbody 2.89s vs 2.15s; Fannkuch 4.24s vs 4.40s (no gain). Static CinderX JIT: Fannkuch 0.84s, Richards 0.88s, nbody 2.31s. Static + Primitives: Fannkuch 0.59s, Richards 0.45s, nbody 0.23s. Ratios (derived from page data): plain CinderX JIT 1.76x Richards, 1.34x nbody, 0.96x Fannkuch; Static + Primitives 8.3x Richards, 12.6x nbody, 7.2x Fannkuch.
hardware: x64 Linux Broadwell 2GHz machine (exact CPU model not stated)
stars_or_usage: 282 stars; used in production at Meta for the Instagram Django service; weekly PyPI releases
tradeoffs: Requires stock CPython 3.14 (below 3.16 on PyPI), GCC 13+ or Clang 18+; experimental for external users per the README. Linux and Windows x86-64, Linux and macOS aarch64. The Static Python columns need type-annotated code compiled with the Static Python compiler, so they are not a drop-in speedup for ordinary Python. The JIT compiles only hot functions after cinderx.jit.auto(); compiling everything can slow short programs (old Cinder README).
caveats: The current repo README and PyPI page contain no benchmark numbers. The only table is in cinderx/website/docs/introduction.md: three micro-benchmarks, Python version of the baseline not stated, no compiler or flags, CPU only described as Broadwell 2GHz, and the JIT is slower on Fannkuch (4.40s vs 4.24s). The repo ships a benchmark harness (cinderx/benchmarks, including fastmark.py for the full pyperformance suite and runner.py) but no committed pyperformance results; I found no independent measurement of CinderX against CPython 3.14. Older first-party claims sit in the cinder/3.10 branch README.rst of facebookincubator/cinder (opened): 'can achieve 1.5-4x speed improvements on many Python performance benchmarks' and 'Static Python plus Cinder JIT achieves 18x the performance of stock CPython on a typed version of the Richards benchmark'; those measured the old CPython 3.10 fork before the 3.11+ adaptive interpreter and are not CinderX-on-3.14 numbers. The same README reports Instagram gains of about 5% from immortal instances and about 5% from awaited-call optimisation, which are not JIT figures. The facebookincubator/cinder main page is now a CPython 3.14 fork (3.8k stars, PSF license) and no longer carries those claims.

name: lumen (Rust JavaScript engine with ARM64 template JIT)
baseline: QuickJS (bellard, version 2026.06.04 in the CI table); V8 and JavaScriptCore are NOT beaten
workload: Classic V8 v7 benchmark suite composite score (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes), higher is better, run nightly in GitHub Actions across engines.
claimed_speedup: ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark macOS-arm64 table (run dated 10/5/2026): lumen 3953 vs QuickJS 1761, quickjs-ng 1660, hermes 1233, i.e. 2.24x QuickJS (derived from page data). Same table: JavaScriptCore 67664, v8 64220, bun 46772, node 37405, so lumen is about 16x below V8 (derived from page data). Ubuntu table: lumen 444 vs QuickJS 1217 (0.36x, lumen slower), v8 48107.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated; the workflow installs engines through the ahaoboy/js-engine-setup action and runs the v8-v7 suite (fork of mozilla/arewefastyet benchmarks/v8-v7); lumen build flags not stated
hardware: GitHub Actions runners macos-latest (arm64) and ubuntu-latest, scheduled daily; CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 271 stars; used as the JS backend of lucid-softworks/browser
tradeoffs: std-only, zero third-party dependencies, three execution tiers (tree-walker, bytecode VM, template JIT; jit is default). Full inline fast paths exist only in the ARM64 JIT backend; the x86-64 backend is 'correctness-first' with native control flow and checked helpers. Other architectures degrade to the bytecode VM. Passes 100% of test262 (53,400/53,400, README). Release binary is about 8 to 11 MB (about 3 MB of it Intl/CLDR data); no https in fetch.
caveats: The README makes no speed claim; the claim here comes only from a third-party engine shootout. The advantage over QuickJS appears on the macOS arm64 runner only; on the Ubuntu x86-64 runner lumen scores 444 against QuickJS 1217, so it is slower there. It is far behind JIT engines (V8, JavaScriptCore, Node, Bun) on both platforms. Lumen's own docs/closure-numeric-regions.md says Djot takes about 15.5x Node's time and 23.9x Bun's, and docs/closure-call-cache.md says the 'within-2x Node/Bun objective remains unmet'. The shootout's lumen version column reads 0.1.3.f6c9860 and the GitHub Actions CPU model is not recorded. The lead said V8 and QuickJS baselines; only QuickJS (an interpreter) is beaten, and only on arm64.

name: CRuby RTL + MJIT (vnmakarov/ruby rtl_mjit_branch)
baseline: Ruby MRI 2.0 (primary) and Ruby MRI 2.5-development trunk the branch is based on ('base')
workload: 23 microbenchmarks from MJIT-benchmarks (while, nest-while, ivread, aref, fib, fannk, sieve, mandelbrot, meteor, nbody, norm, trees, pent, red-black, bench, ...) plus the optcarrot NES emulator at 180 and 2000 frames; wall time, CPU time and peak memory, minimum of 3 runs.
claimed_speedup: Wall-time geometric mean speedup over MRI 2.0 across the 23 microbenchmarks: mjit (GCC 6.3.1 -O2) 6.18x, mjit-cl (Clang 3.9.1 -O2) 4.02x, rtl insns without JIT 1.39x, base MRI 2.5-dev 1.12x (so mjit is about 5.5x over base, derived from page data). Optcarrot 2000 frames: 28.96 FPS MRI 2.0, 39.43 FPS base, 78.22 FPS mjit (2.7x), 90.58 FPS mjit-cl (3.13x); default 180 frames: 82.06 FPS mjit (2.83x), 85.43 FPS mjit-cl (2.94x). CPU-time geomean 5.55x for mjit. Optcarrot against base is about 1.98x (mjit) and 2.30x (mjit-cl) at 2000 frames (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: MJIT-generated C compiled with GCC 6.3.1 -O2 (mjit) or LLVM Clang 3.9.1 -O2 (mjit-cl); build flags of the MRI 2.0 and base interpreters not stated
hardware: Intel 3.9GHz i3-7100, 32GB memory, x86-64 Fedora Core 25
tradeoffs: Method JIT that generates C code and runs GCC or Clang at runtime, loading the result as a shared object from /tmp; needs a C compiler installed at run time. Compiling a small ISEQ takes about 50-70 ms. Peak memory geomean 4.15x (GCC) and 6.44x (Clang) of MRI 2.0 including the compiler. README says it is at a very early stage and only ready for a few small, simple Ruby programs (June 2017 update).
caveats: Numbers are from June 2017 on a prototype branch, last commit 2017-09-29; the branch is not maintained. The headline 6.18x is against Ruby 2.0, an old baseline; against the 2.5-development trunk it is about 5.5x, and the 'while' microbenchmark (387x for GCC mjit) skews the geomean. Build flags of the baseline MRI binaries are not stated (hence verifier may downgrade A to C). Optcarrot is the only real-program result: 2.7x to 3.13x over MRI 2.0, about 2x over base, and CPU time gain only 1.49x to 1.53x. Benchmark scripts are in the branch under MJIT-benchmarks (compare.rb, optcarrot-compare.rb). Not the same as the later JIT shipped in released Ruby; I did not evaluate that. vnmakarov/mir is already catalogued and is not duplicated here.

name: Topaz (Ruby on RPython; measured on the kostya/topaz fork)
workload: Thirteen simplified Benchmarks Game style programs (binarytrees, brainfuck, brainfuck2, fannkuchredux, fasta, knucleotide, mandelbrot, matmul, nbody, pidigits, regexdna, revcomp, spectralnorm); best of up to 5 runs, time measured inside the language, in seconds.
claimed_speedup: kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (2023-02-28), best seconds Topaz vs Ruby 2.7 vs Ruby 3.2 (no JIT): binarytrees 1.97 vs 6.75 vs 6.16; brainfuck 17.41 vs 115.31 vs 118.9; brainfuck2 22.71 vs 93.93 vs 90.85; fannkuchredux 0.43 vs 4.34 vs 4.3; fasta 5.29 vs 18.19 vs 16.21; knucleotide 5.25 vs 11.02 vs 11.6; mandelbrot 1.47 vs 16.74 vs 20.86; matmul 1.83 vs 18.39 vs 20.88; nbody 5.42 vs 43.56 vs 49.92; pidigits 7.78 vs 11.42 vs 10.64; regexdna 3.1 vs 6.25 vs 7.46; spectralnorm 1.44 vs 17.18 vs 15.25; revcomp 7.3 vs 4.2 vs 3.67 (Topaz slower). Ratios (derived from page data): geomean about 4.2x over Ruby 2.7 and 4.3x over Ruby 3.2 across the 13; up to 11.9x (spectralnorm) and 11.4x (mandelbrot) over Ruby 2.7; faster in 12 of 13.
compiler_and_flags: Topaz translated with rpython -Ojit on PyPy 2.7 v7.3.6 inside Docker (docker/topaz); CRuby built from source with a plain ./configure and make (docker/ruby2); gcc 12.2.0 for the C reference; no extra optimisation flags given
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 80GB DDR4-3200, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10
stars_or_usage: 1.0k stars (topazproject/topaz); the measured fork kostya/topaz is a fork of it
tradeoffs: Implements Ruby on RPython; the README does not state which Ruby version or how much of CRuby 2.7 or 3.x it covers, so compatibility is unverified. Translation with RPython takes 5-10 minutes and needs a PyPy source tree at tag release-2.4.0 per the upstream README. Memory use is higher than CRuby on allocation heavy runs (binarytrees 63.1 MB vs 44.6 MB Ruby 2.7 in the same table).
caveats: The measured binary is built from kostya/topaz (a fork of the unmaintained upstream; last commit 2023-01-27, 'update to pypy7.3.2' and 'change default hash implementation which is faster'), not upstream topazproject/topaz, whose last commit is 2022-06-18. The upstream README states goals of simplicity and performance but publishes no numbers. The benchmark programs are deliberately simple and single-threaded, so Topaz's lack of full compatibility is not exercised. Several slow Ruby cells have only 1 or 2 runs (e.g. brainfuck, nbody), and each program reports its own elapsed time (the harness reads a time(TIME) line from stderr), so interpreter startup and compile time are excluded. revcomp is slower on Topaz (7.3s vs 4.2s). Kostya notes his own README says the numbers are not final performance. The suite is the third-party community shootout kostya/jit-benchmarks (MIT, 104 stars, last update 2023-02-28).

name: Quirrel (Gaijin Entertainment Squirrel fork)
baseline: Squirrel 3.2 (original); also measured against Lua 5.5.1, LuaJIT 2.1 with -joff, Luau 0.735, QuickJS-ng 0.16.2
workload: Thirteen interpreter workloads (n-bodies, particles-kinematics, exp-loop, dictionary, darg-ui-benchmark, fibonacci recursive and loop, primes-loop, float2string, queen, sort, spectral-norm, string2float), best time per cell over 3 processes pinned to one core, seconds, lower is better.
claimed_speedup: doc/content/_bench.json (Quirrel-4.38.0 vs Squirrel-3.2, seconds): particles-kinematics 0.211 vs 0.36; primes-loop 0.099 vs 0.173; spectral-norm 0.475 vs 0.657; fibonacci-recursive 0.097 vs 0.133; fibonacci-loop 0.035 vs 0.048; n-bodies 0.867 vs 1.075; darg-ui-benchmark 0.351 vs 0.468; sort 0.085 vs 0.11; faster in 12 of 13 workloads (float2string 0.044 vs 0.0409999 is the exception), geomean about 1.28x over Squirrel 3.2 (derived from page data). Against Lua-5.5.1 Quirrel is slower: geomean about 0.87x, faster in only 3 of 13 (particles-kinematics 0.211 vs 0.381, fibonacci-loop 0.035 vs 0.037, float2string 0.044 vs 0.458); against LuaJIT -joff about 0.51x; against QuickJS-ng about 1.56x faster (derived from page data). README text: 'equal performance to Lua'.
compiler_and_flags: Quirrel: release build of the Dagor tree interpreter, clang with mimalloc (jam -sConfig=rel); third-party interpreters built with clang-cl (LLVM 21.1.8) /O2 /MT, Lua with -DLUA_USE_JUMPTABLE=1; LuaJIT with cl via msvcbuild.bat static and run with -joff
hardware: Windows 11 x64, Intel64 Family 6 Model 183 Stepping 1 (GenuineIntel; marketing name not stated), pinned to one P-core, run dated 2026-09-03
stars_or_usage: 223 stars; README says used in dozens of games and apps with hundreds of millions of installations (first-party statement)
tradeoffs: Stricter and safer than Squirrel by design (README), so not guaranteed to be a drop-in replacement for Squirrel scripts; C/Java-like syntax with Lua-like dynamism; no JIT by design (targets consoles and phones). Standalone repo is synced in batches from the Dagor engine tree.
caveats: First-party benchmark. The Quirrel binary is the shipped configuration with mimalloc, while the repo bench README says a CRT-heap build is up to 2x slower on table-sweep workloads, so part of the margin over the Squirrel 3.2 baseline may be allocator rather than VM; how sq3-64.exe was built is described only as upstream sources built with clang-cl /O2 /MT. Quirrel loses to Lua 5.5.1 overall in its own table and in the daslang dasProfile README (borisbat/dasProfile, Quirrel 4.29.1 vs Lua 5.5.1: geomean 0.89x on Apple M1 Max and 0.94x on Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE, derived from page data; that suite has no Squirrel column and is written by a Gaijin-affiliated project). The README claim 'equal performance to Lua' is therefore roughly true and the only clear win is over Squirrel. CPU identified only as Intel Family 6 Model 183; the verifier may upgrade C to A if that counts as a stated CPU model. Benchmark sources are in DagorEngine under prog/1stPartyLibs/quirrel/quirrel/bench (benchmarks.py, run_vm_bench.py).

name: Porffor (AOT JavaScript/TypeScript to Wasm and C)
baseline: QuickJS and Node --jitless (V8 interpreter only); Node and Bun with JIT are NOT beaten
workload: V8 benchmark suite (v8-v7) composite score, higher is better; the suite is committed as bench/v8-v7.js.
claimed_speedup: Snippet of the porffor.dev site (page blocked, not opened): Porffor 6,646 vs Node without JIT 5,828, Bun without JIT 4,464, QuickJS 3,564; Node and Bun with JIT score 13 to 17x higher. Ratios (derived from the snippet): 1.14x Node jitless, 1.86x QuickJS.
tradeoffs: 100% AOT: compiles JS to C (with an IR) and also Wasm, with nothing interpreted or JIT-compiled; supports a subset of ECMA-262 (the README gives no conformance figure). Strong on startup, memory and binary size per the site, not on peak speed.
caveats: Snippet only: the numbers come from a WebSearch snippet that quotes porffor.dev; the site is blocked by egress policy so hardware, versions, flags and date could not be read, hence no benchmark_url and tier C at most. The committed repo README has no numbers (only 'compiled hello.js in 105ms, 33.7KB'). The README no longer says pre-alpha. Porffor is far slower than JIT-enabled V8 and JavaScriptCore on the same suite, so the win is over Node's interpreter-only mode and QuickJS. Third-party harness jlucaso1/js-compiled (also proggeramlug/js-compiled) benchmarks Porffor vs Node, Bun and scriptc on 22 programs, but its results are published only on GitHub Pages (blocked) and are not committed. The bench/ directory has 26 benchmark programs (richards.js, v8-v7.js and more) but no results file.

name: scriptc (Vercel Labs TypeScript to native compiler)
baseline: Node.js 24.18.0 (V8) and Bun 1.3.12; slower than both on sustained throughput per the same reports
workload: CLI process startup (median) of a compiled scriptc 0.0.16 executable against the same program on Bun and Node, plus idle memory of a node:http server.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: median CLI startup 1.78 ms for scriptc vs 21.29 ms for Bun 1.3.12 and 61.78 ms for Node 24.18.0 (about 12x and 35x, derived from the snippet); idle memory 1.9 MiB for a framework-free node:http server. Same coverage says Hono needs --dynamic and reaches 18.4k requests per second vs 70.5k for Bun.
tradeoffs: Compiles a typed subset of TypeScript/JavaScript and Node APIs to native code through LLVM, with no JS engine in static builds; --dynamic embeds quickjs-ng for npm dependencies and any-typed code and then loses the native speed. Runtime semantics differ from Node (see docs limitations page); experimental per the README.
caveats: Snippet only: the startup numbers come from WebSearch result snippets of news coverage (InfoQ and other outlets, all blocked here), whose original source and hardware I could not open; neither the scriptc README nor docs nor release notes contain a Node or Bun comparison. The repo has benchmarks/builds and scripts/bench-builds.mjs, which measure build latency and executable run time, not a Node or Bun comparison. Throughput is the weak side: GitHub issue titles (opened in the issue search page) say 'Bitwise operators lower to out-of-line scr_bit_* calls: 77x slower than Node on integer hot loops' (#357) and 'f64 loop indices prevent vectorization: byte loops still 2-6x slower than Node' (#113); later issues (e.g. #358) work on these, so figures may be stale. A search snippet also quotes one developer measuring about 7.5x slower than Node 24. Third-party harnesses (proggeramlug/js-compiled and jlucaso1/js-compiled) benchmark scriptc against Node, Bun and Porffor on 22 programs, but results are only on GitHub Pages (blocked) and not committed. Notable at 6k stars, so recorded despite thin evidence; tier C only because the snippets give numbers.
